slides.title: Get started
slides.html:
Show the fins illusion. Everyone writes which segment is longer and how sure they are (1 to 5), then measures. Tally the class guesses against the measurement. The fins figure is called the Müller-Lyer illusion. Psychologists still study why it fools us. The segments are equal every time.

geo.title: Get started
geo.body:
Show the fins illusion. Everyone writes which segment is longer and how sure they are (1 to 5), then measures. Tally the class guesses against the measurement. The fins figure is called the Müller-Lyer illusion. Psychologists still study why it fools us. The segments are equal every time.

  • I can explain why we question what our eyes tell us.
  • I can sort statements about a figure into observed, measured, assumed and proved.
  • I can explain why an optical illusion is a reason to prove, not just look.

slides.title: The big idea
slides.html: A drawing helps us think, but it is not evidence. A solution may use only four kinds of facts: what we are given, what we measured with a stated tool, what we openly assume, and what we prove.

geo.title: The big idea
geo.body: A drawing helps us think, but it is not evidence. A solution may use only four kinds of facts: what we are given, what we measured with a stated tool, what we openly assume, and what we prove.

slides.title: Words to know
slides.html:
• given A fact we are told to accept at the start of a problem.
  • measurement A number found with a tool, like a ruler or protractor, with a unit.
  • assumption Something we accept without checking. Good work says its assumptions out loud.
  • proof A chain of reasons that shows a statement must be true.
  • not to scale The drawing's sizes may be wrong, so use the labels, not your eyes.

slides.title: Worked example
slides.html:
Do these two segments have to be equal?

Read the worked steps
StepReason
Look at what the sketch tells us. There are no tick marks and no lengths written.A tick mark or a written length would be a given. Here there is none.
So 'they are equal' is not a given. It only looks that way.How a picture looks is not information.
Measure with a ruler we trust. One segment runs from 0 to 3. The other runs from 5 to 8.A stated measurement counts as information.
Both lengths are 3, so now we know they are equal.3 - 0 = 3 and 8 - 5 = 3.
With no ruler, we would need a tick mark, a stated assumption or a proof.Those are the only ways a fact gets into a solution.
Second check: redraw one segment a little longer. Nothing we were told is broken, but now they are not equal.So the picture alone could never settle it.

slides.title: Worked example
slides.html:
Zooming in does not change the length.

Read the worked steps
StepReason
The sheet says AB = 7 cm.This is a given.
The screen shows the drawing 2 times as big.Zooming changes the picture, not the problem.
Use 7 cm in the solution.Only the given counts.
To use 14 cm, the problem would have to say the real segment was doubled.A new fact needs a new given.
Second check: print the same sheet at two zoom sizes. It still says AB = 7 cm both times.Same given, same answer.

slides.title: Try it
slides.html: Illusion lab: drag the arrow fins on two segments. The segments seem to change length, but the length readout never moves. Write one sentence on what changed and what stayed the same.

slides.title: Common mistake
slides.html:
Sam writes 'angle 1 = angle 2, because they look the same.' There are no marks and no measurements.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Find and fix the error

Looks are not a reason. Sam needs a matching mark, a measurement, an assumption the problem states, or a proof.

slides.title: Practice 1
slides.html:
A route note says M is between P and Q, two different points. The drawing puts the dot for M off segment PQ. What can you conclude: M is on segment PQ, PM = MQ, or both? Should you fix the picture or the note?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

Only 'M is on segment PQ.' Between means M sits on the segment, strictly inside it. Nothing says the two parts are equal. Fix the picture so it agrees with the note. A dot in the wrong place can't cancel a given.

Reveal second check

Cover the picture and read the note: M is still on the segment. To test PM = MQ, put P at 0, M at 2 and Q at 6 on a number line. The order is right, but PM = 2 and MQ = 4, so equal parts are not forced.

slides.title: Practice 2
slides.html:
Riley looks at a sketch with no marks and no lengths and writes AB = CD 'because they look equal.' What went wrong? Describe a picture that fits everything you were told, but where AB and CD are not equal.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

Riley used a fact that was never given or proved. Draw AB with length 3 and CD with length 4, with the same letters and no marks. That picture fits all the facts, and the lengths are different.

Reveal second check

Nothing in the problem rules out lengths 3 and 4. One picture that fits the facts and breaks the claim is enough.

slides.title: Practice 3
slides.html:
Always, sometimes or never? Two drawings of the same segment can be different lengths on the screen, and both can still be correct.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

Sometimes. If a drawing is marked 'not to scale' or uses a different scale, the screen lengths can differ and both are fine. If both must use the same scale, the screen lengths must match.

Reveal second check

The answer depends on whether the scale is stated. A pixel count alone never adds a fact about length.

geo.title: Practice 3
geo.prompt: Always, sometimes or never? Two drawings of the same segment can be different lengths on the screen, and both can still be correct.
geo.solution: Sometimes. If a drawing is marked 'not to scale' or uses a different scale, the screen lengths can differ and both are fine. If both must use the same scale, the screen lengths must match.
geo.check: The answer depends on whether the scale is stated. A pixel count alone never adds a fact about length.

slides.title: Check yourself
slides.html:
Sort these: 'It looks like a right angle.' 'The protractor reading is written on the sheet.' 'We assume the floor is flat.' 'We proved it.' Which ones can a solution use?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

The last three: a stated measurement, a stated assumption and a proof. 'It looks like' cannot be used.

Reveal second check

Name the given, measurement, assumption, definition or proof you used.
